interest: Shows US officials critiquing Japan's 1945 Trade Union Law as paternalistic, pushing New Deal-style labor protections.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
overview: Decimal file 894.5043 (File 1517), covering March 28 to April 10, 1946, documents the critical assessment and inter-agency transmission of Japan's initial post-war Trade Union Law (Law No. 51 of December 1945) by U.S. occupation authorities and Washington departments. The core of the file consists of two detailed technical critiques—one by Philip B. Sullivan of the State Department's Division of International Labor, Social and Health Affairs, and an extensive article-by-article analysis by Harold S. Roberts of the U.S. Department of Labor—both warning that the Japanese legislation preserved excessive bureaucratic and administrative control over unions, permitted court dissolution, exposed unions to ruinous liability suits, and failed to meet the democratic standards envisioned in SWNCC 92. Edwin M. Martin of the State Department's Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs forwarded these studies to the War Department to aid SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section in guiding future legislative amendments, while a concluding despatch from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo (drafted by John S. Service) transmitted official Japanese government translations of the Trade Union Law and its February 1946 enforcement ordinances.

subfiles.about: Critical memorandum by State Department labor expert Philip B. Sullivan analyzing the restrictive and bureaucratic nature of Japan's Trade Union Law.
subfiles.from: Philip B. Sullivan (Division of International Labor, Social and Health Affairs, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: Philip B. Sullivan evaluates Japanese Law No. 51 (the Trade Union Law), finding it a distinct disappointment and contrary to the spirit of SWNCC 92. He identifies major defects, including provisions allowing courts to dissolve unions at administrative request (Article 15), administrative power to alter trade agreements (Article 24), prohibitions against political movements and organizing by police and prison guards (Articles 2 and 4), and union vulnerability to bankruptcy through civil damage suits (Articles 12, 14, and 17). Sullivan urges that revisions be ordered promptly and that experienced American trade union advisors be dispatched to assist emerging Japanese labor organizations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Philip B. Sullivan on the Trade Union Law of Japan
subfiles.to: Major William W. Lockwood and Lieutenant Owen (Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State)

subfiles.about: Exhaustive section-by-section analysis and proposed statutory revisions of Japan's Trade Union Law by Harold S. Roberts of the Department of Labor.
subfiles.from: Harold S. Roberts (Assistant Director, Division of Industrial Relations, Department of Labor)
subfiles.summary: Harold S. Roberts provides a comprehensive article-by-article critique of the Japanese Trade Union Law, arguing that its mandatory registration and extensive administrative oversight create a bureaucratic stranglehold that will stifle a free labor movement. Drawing heavily on the U.S. National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act), the Norris-LaGuardia Act, and British trade union precedents, Roberts supplies draft language to guarantee majority exclusive representation, ban employer unfair labor practices, and curtail court injunctions and damage suits. He also designs detailed tripartite conciliation, mediation, and voluntary arbitration machinery, proposing that the reformed statute be titled the 'Labor Relations Act of 1946.'
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Harold S. Roberts to Thomas Holland analyzing the Trade Union Law of Japan

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch forwarding GHQ SCAP English translations of Japan's Trade Union Law and related enforcement ordinances.
subfiles.from: John S. Service (Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Tokyo forwards SCAP's English translations of Japan's basic 1945-46 labor-union legislation, not yet fully verified.
